Requirement: Identify the internal and external issues that affect what the ISMS needs to achieve — regulation, market, technology, culture, structure. Since the 2024 amendment, explicitly consider whether climate change is a relevant issue.
What good looks like: A current record of the issues that shape the ISMS, revisited after significant business change rather than only at audit time, with climate change explicitly considered.

Requirement: List the parties that care about your information security (customers, regulators, staff, suppliers, shareholders), what they require, and which of those requirements the ISMS will address. Their requirements may include climate-related expectations.
What good looks like: A register that names the parties, states their requirements concretely, and distinguishes the requirements the ISMS addresses from those it does not.

Requirement: Decide and document the boundaries of the ISMS — locations, functions, systems, services — taking the issues, requirements and interfaces with other organisations into account.
What good looks like: A documented scope covering locations, functions, systems and services, with exclusions justified and shared interfaces analysed rather than ignored.

Requirement: Establish, implement, maintain and continually improve the ISMS, including the processes it needs and how they interact.
What good looks like: The ISMS is described as a set of interacting processes with owners, not as a folder of documents.

Requirement: Top management shows commitment by aligning the ISMS with strategy, integrating it into business processes, providing resources, communicating its importance and supporting others in their roles.
What good looks like: Decisions, resourcing and attendance records that show named senior people engaging with security — not a signature on a policy and nothing else.

Requirement: Top management sets an information security policy that fits the organisation, provides a framework for objectives, commits to meeting requirements and to continual improvement, and is documented, communicated and available.
What good looks like: An approved, version-controlled policy that is published where staff can find it, with acknowledgement records and a review history.

Requirement: Top management assigns and communicates security responsibilities and authorities, including who makes sure the ISMS conforms to the standard and who reports on its performance.
What good looks like: Roles assigned to named people with the authority and time to act, kept current through leavers and restructures, and confirmed in interview.

Requirement: Using the context and requirements from Clause 4, determine the risks and opportunities the ISMS must address so it achieves its outcomes and prevents undesired effects, and plan how to act on them.
What good looks like: Planning that addresses threats to the management system achieving its outcomes, not only threats to information assets.

Requirement: Define and apply a risk assessment process with risk acceptance criteria and criteria for performing assessments, that produces consistent, valid and comparable results; identify risks and their owners, analyse likelihood and consequence, and evaluate them against the criteria.
What good looks like: A documented, repeatable method with a defined scale and criteria, applied consistently across the register by named risk owners.

Requirement: Select treatment options, determine the controls needed, compare them with Annex A so nothing necessary is missed, produce a Statement of Applicability, write a risk treatment plan, and obtain risk owners' approval of the plan and the residual risks.
What good looks like: A treatment plan traceable from risk to control to evidence, a Statement of Applicability justifying every control both ways, and residual risk accepted by someone with authority.

Requirement: Set measurable objectives consistent with the policy, then plan what will be done, with what resources, by whom, by when, and how results will be evaluated.
What good looks like: Objectives that are measurable and resourced, tracked with real numbers, with a visible response when a target is not met.

Requirement: New in 2022: when the ISMS needs to change, the change must be carried out in a planned way rather than ad hoc.
What good looks like: Change planning that routinely asks the security question in advance, with evidence from recent real changes rather than a documented intention.

Requirement: Determine and provide the people, budget, tools and infrastructure needed to establish, run and improve the ISMS.
What good looks like: Resourcing that matches the commitments in the ISMS, with shortfalls acknowledged and escalated rather than absorbed silently.

Requirement: Decide what competence people whose work affects security need, make sure they have it through education, training or experience, act to close gaps, check that the action worked, and keep evidence.
What good looks like: Competence defined per role and evidenced by training, qualification or demonstrated experience, with gaps addressed.

Requirement: People working under the organisation's control must know the policy, how they contribute to the ISMS, and what happens if they do not conform.
What good looks like: Awareness activity that reaches everyone, repeats, is tailored to real risks, and has completion records.

Requirement: Decide what to communicate about information security, when, with whom, and how — internally and externally.
What good looks like: Communication that is planned rather than ad hoc, including who may speak externally about a security incident.

Requirement: Keep the documented information the standard requires and whatever else the ISMS needs; create it with proper identification, format and review; and control it so it is available when needed and protected from loss, misuse and unauthorised change.
What good looks like: Documents carry owners, versions and approval; records are retained for a defined period and are retrievable on request.

Requirement: Plan, implement and control the processes needed to meet requirements and carry out the Clause 6 actions; set criteria for those processes, control planned changes, review the effects of unintended ones, and control externally provided processes, products and services.
What good looks like: Operational records from the live process, not a description of how it is supposed to work.

Requirement: Carry out risk assessments at planned intervals and whenever significant changes are proposed or happen, using the Clause 6.1.2 criteria, and keep the results.
What good looks like: Risk assessment on a defined schedule and after significant change, with the results feeding the treatment plan and the register dated.

Requirement: Implement the risk treatment plan and keep evidence of the results.
What good looks like: A treatment plan where completed items can be evidenced and slipped items have revised dates and a reason.

Requirement: Decide what to monitor and measure, the methods (which should give comparable and reproducible results), when, and who analyses and evaluates the results — then evaluate security performance and ISMS effectiveness and keep evidence.
What good looks like: Defined metrics with a method and a frequency, analysed to a conclusion that drives action — not numbers collected and filed.

Requirement: Audit the ISMS at planned intervals against the organisation's own requirements and the standard, under an audit programme that sets frequency, methods, responsibilities and reporting; choose auditors who are objective and impartial, and report results to relevant management.
What good looks like: A risk-based programme with demonstrated coverage, auditors who do not audit their own work, and findings that reach the corrective action log.

Requirement: Top management reviews the ISMS at planned intervals, considering defined inputs — previous actions, changes in context, interested parties' needs, performance trends, audit results, risk status and improvement opportunities — and records decisions on improvement and needed changes.
What good looks like: Minutes at planned intervals showing top management present, every required input covered, and decisions with owners and dates.

Requirement: Continually improve how suitable, adequate and effective the ISMS is.
What good looks like: Specific improvements traceable to audits, incidents, metrics or reviews — evidence of a system that changes, not one that is merely maintained.

Requirement: When a nonconformity occurs, react to control and correct it, deal with consequences, find the root cause and whether it could happen elsewhere, act to prevent recurrence, check the action worked, update the ISMS if needed, and keep records.
What good looks like: Root causes that reach a process or design decision, corrective actions that address that cause, and a recorded effectiveness check after the event.

Requirement: Sets the direction for information security in writing. A top-level policy approved by management, supported by topic-specific policies, tells everyone what the organisation expects and gives every other control a mandate to point back to.
What good looks like: Approved, version-controlled policy documents with owners and review dates; Records of management approval (board minutes, signed approval page or workflow log)

Requirement: Makes sure every security responsibility has a named owner. Without explicit allocation, tasks such as risk ownership, asset ownership and incident handling fall between teams.
What good looks like: A roles and responsibilities document or RACI covering the ISMS; Job descriptions that include security duties for key roles

Requirement: Reduces the chance of error or fraud by making sure no single person can complete a sensitive process end to end without a check by someone else.
What good looks like: A documented list of conflicting duties and how each is separated; Role and permission configurations in key systems (ERP, IAM, CI/CD)

Requirement: Requires managers to actively make staff follow security policies and procedures, rather than treating security as the security team's job alone.
What good looks like: Management communications reinforcing security expectations; Training completion tracked and chased by line managers

Requirement: Ensures the organisation knows which authorities to contact — regulators, law enforcement, data protection authorities — and can reach them quickly when an incident or legal obligation requires it.
What good looks like: A maintained register of authority contacts with owners and review dates; Incident or breach procedures that reference when and how to notify authorities

Requirement: Keeps the security team connected to professional forums, industry groups and information-sharing communities so it learns about emerging threats and good practice early.
What good looks like: A list of memberships and subscriptions with owners; Examples where information from these groups changed a control or prompted action

Requirement: Collects and analyses information about threats relevant to the organisation so defences and risk decisions are based on what attackers are actually doing, not guesswork.
What good looks like: A documented threat intelligence process with sources and owners; Intelligence reports or summaries produced for different audiences

Requirement: Builds security into projects from the start, so risks are assessed and requirements agreed before money is spent and designs are fixed — not bolted on before go-live.
What good looks like: Project methodology documents showing security gates; Risk assessments and security requirements for recent projects

Requirement: You cannot protect what you do not know you have. An accurate inventory of information and the systems, devices and services that hold it is the foundation for risk assessment and most other controls.
What good looks like: The asset inventory with owners, classifications and last-updated dates; Reconciliation records against network scans, MDM or cloud console exports

Requirement: Tells people clearly what they may and may not do with the organisation's information, devices and services, so expectations are known and breaches can be acted on.
What good looks like: The acceptable use policy and handling rules; Signed or electronic acknowledgements from users

Requirement: Makes sure laptops, phones, access cards and information held by leavers and departing contractors come back to the organisation when the relationship ends or changes.
What good looks like: Leaver checklists showing assets returned and signed off; Inventory updates matching returned equipment

Requirement: Groups information by sensitivity so protection matches the harm its loss or exposure would cause — spending effort where it matters instead of treating everything the same.
What good looks like: A classification scheme with criteria and handling rules; Classified entries in the asset inventory

Requirement: Puts a visible or machine-readable label on information so people and systems know how to handle it — the practical follow-through of classification.
What good looks like: Labelling procedures for each format; Sample documents and emails carrying the correct labels

Requirement: Protects information when it moves — by email, file transfer, removable media, courier or conversation — whether inside the organisation or to outside parties.
What good looks like: Information transfer rules or procedures; Secure transfer tools in use (encrypted email, managed file transfer)

Requirement: Sets the rules for who may access what, based on business need and least privilege. It is the policy layer; identity, authentication and access rights controls put it into practice.
What good looks like: An access control policy approved by management; Role definitions or access matrices for key systems

Requirement: Manages the full life cycle of identities — people, service accounts and devices — so every access can be traced to a unique, valid identity.
What good looks like: Joiner-mover-leaver procedures linked to HR events; Identity lists from directories with owners for service accounts

Requirement: Controls how passwords, PINs, keys and other secrets are issued and handled, so they cannot easily be guessed, shared or stolen.
What good looks like: Password and authentication policy; System configuration showing password settings and hashing

Requirement: Makes sure access is granted with approval, reviewed regularly and removed promptly, so people only keep the access they still need.
What good looks like: Access request and approval records; Completed access reviews with actions taken

Requirement: Manages the risk that comes with suppliers who access, process or affect your information — from selection through to exit.
What good looks like: Supplier security policy and risk tiering criteria; Supplier register with risk ratings

Requirement: Turns security requirements into contractual obligations so suppliers are bound to protect your information and you have rights to verify and enforce it.
What good looks like: Contract templates with security clauses; Signed agreements for critical suppliers containing those clauses

Requirement: Addresses risks deeper in the supply chain — the components, software and sub-suppliers your ICT suppliers depend on.
What good looks like: Contract clauses requiring flow-down of security requirements; Lists of sub-processors or critical components for key services

Requirement: Keeps supplier security under watch after the contract is signed, and manages the risk when a supplier changes its service.
What good looks like: Supplier review records and meeting minutes; Collected certificates or assurance reports (for example SOC 2, ISO 27001) with expiry tracking

Requirement: Governs how cloud services are bought, used, managed and exited, recognising that security is shared between the organisation and the cloud provider.
What good looks like: Cloud security policy and approved service list; Shared responsibility matrices for key services

Requirement: Prepares the organisation to handle incidents before they happen: defined roles, procedures, contacts and tools ready to use under pressure.
What good looks like: The incident management plan and playbooks; Up-to-date contact and escalation lists

Requirement: Decides consistently which reported events are actual incidents, so real incidents get a response and noise does not overwhelm the team.
What good looks like: Triage criteria and severity definitions; Event and incident logs showing decisions and timestamps

Requirement: Responds to incidents according to documented procedures, so containment, eradication, recovery and communication happen quickly and consistently.
What good looks like: Incident tickets or reports showing actions and timelines; Communications and notifications sent

Requirement: Uses what incidents reveal to strengthen controls and reduce the chance or impact of the next one.
What good looks like: Post-incident review reports; Action trackers showing completed improvements

Requirement: Collects and preserves evidence about incidents in a way that would stand up in disciplinary, legal or regulatory proceedings.
What good looks like: Evidence handling procedures; Chain of custody forms from past incidents

Requirement: Keeps information security at an appropriate level during a crisis or disruption, when normal processes are under strain and shortcuts are tempting.
What good looks like: Continuity plans that address security requirements; Exercise reports covering security during disruption

Requirement: Makes sure IT services can be recovered within the times the business needs, based on business impact analysis.
What good looks like: Business impact analysis with RTO/RPO values; ICT continuity and recovery plans

Requirement: Identifies the laws, regulations and contractual obligations that affect information security, and keeps them up to date so the ISMS meets them.
What good looks like: Legal and contractual requirements register with owners and review dates; Mapping of requirements to controls

Requirement: Protects intellectual property — the organisation's own and that of others — and ensures software and content are used within licence terms.
What good looks like: Software asset management or licence records; Policy on software installation and open-source use

Requirement: Protects records from loss, destruction, falsification and unauthorised access, and keeps them for as long as law, contract and business need require.
What good looks like: Records retention schedule; Storage and access controls for key records

Requirement: Meets privacy and data protection obligations for personally identifiable information (PII) across its whole life cycle.
What good looks like: Privacy policy and record of processing activities; Data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing

Requirement: Has the organisation's approach to security reviewed by someone independent of the area being reviewed, at planned intervals and after significant change.
What good looks like: Independent review plans and reports; Evidence of reviewer independence

Requirement: Checks regularly that the organisation actually follows its own security policies, rules and standards — and acts when it does not.
What good looks like: Compliance check records and results; Technical compliance reports

Requirement: Documents how information processing facilities are operated, so tasks are done consistently, securely and by more than one person.
What good looks like: Operating procedures with owners and review dates; Evidence procedures are followed (logs, checklists, tickets)

Requirement: Checks the background of people before they join, proportionate to the role, the information they will access and the law — so trust is earned before access is granted.
What good looks like: Screening policy with checks per role category; Completed screening records for a sample of recent joiners (held securely by HR)

Requirement: Puts each person's information security responsibilities into their employment or engagement contract, so obligations are agreed and enforceable from day one.
What good looks like: Contract templates with security clauses; Signed contracts for a sample of staff and contractors

Requirement: Gives people the knowledge they need to protect information in their role — not one induction slide deck, but ongoing awareness plus deeper training where roles need it.
What good looks like: Awareness and training plan with audiences and frequency; Completion records, with overdue training followed up

Requirement: Provides a fair, known process for dealing with people who breach security policy, which both deters breaches and makes the response consistent.
What good looks like: HR disciplinary policy referencing security breaches; Communication of the process (handbook, training)

Requirement: Makes sure security obligations that outlast employment — such as confidentiality — are communicated and enforced when someone leaves or changes role.
What good looks like: Exit checklist and leaver letters referencing ongoing obligations; Access removal and asset return records for recent leavers

Requirement: Uses confidentiality or non-disclosure agreements to protect information shared with staff, contractors and third parties, reflecting what actually needs protecting.
What good looks like: NDA templates reviewed by legal; Signed NDAs for a sample of contractors and partners

Requirement: Protects information accessed, processed or stored outside the organisation's premises — at home, while travelling or in shared spaces.
What good looks like: Remote working policy; Device management and secure access configurations

Requirement: Gives everyone a quick, easy way to report suspected security events, so problems are found early by the people who see them first.
What good looks like: Published reporting channels and guidance; Records of reported events and their handling

Requirement: Defines and protects the physical boundaries around areas that hold information and processing facilities, so unauthorised people cannot simply walk in.
What good looks like: Site plans showing defined secure areas; Physical inspection of doors, windows and access points

Requirement: Controls who can enter secure areas through entry points — staff, visitors and deliveries — so only authorised people get in.
What good looks like: Access control system configuration and access lists; Visitor logs and visitor badge process

Requirement: Applies physical security to the offices, rooms and facilities inside the perimeter, especially those that hold sensitive information or equipment.
What good looks like: Inspection of locks and room security; Key and access code registers

Requirement: Continuously monitors premises for unauthorised physical access, so intrusions are detected and responded to rather than discovered later.
What good looks like: Monitoring system coverage and maintenance records; Alarm response procedures and logs

Requirement: Protects facilities against natural and man-made threats — fire, flood, heat, power surges, storms, civil unrest — based on a realistic assessment of the site.
What good looks like: Site risk assessment covering environmental threats; Fire suppression and detection test records

Requirement: Sets rules for behaviour inside secure areas, so the controls that protect them are not undermined by the people working there.
What good looks like: Secure area working rules; Supervision records for third-party work

Requirement: Reduces exposure of information left on desks and screens, including printed material, removable media and unlocked sessions.
What good looks like: Clear desk and clear screen policy; Screen lock configuration in device management

Requirement: Places and protects equipment to reduce risks from environmental threats and unauthorised access or viewing.
What good looks like: Inspection of equipment placement and racks; Positioning of screens in public or shared areas

Requirement: Protects equipment and information taken outside the organisation's premises, where theft, loss and overlooking are more likely.
What good looks like: Off-site equipment rules; Device encryption and remote wipe status from device management

Requirement: Manages removable and other storage media through its life — acquisition, use, transport, re-use and disposal — so information on it is not lost or exposed.
What good looks like: Removable media policy and technical enforcement settings; Media register for sensitive media

Requirement: Protects information processing facilities from failures of supporting utilities such as power, cooling and telecommunications.
What good looks like: UPS and generator test and maintenance records; Utility monitoring alerts

Requirement: Protects power and data cabling from interception, interference and damage.
What good looks like: Cabling documentation and labelling; Locked patch panels and cabinets

Requirement: Keeps equipment correctly maintained so it stays available and secure, and makes sure maintenance itself does not expose information.
What good looks like: Maintenance schedules and service records; Approved maintenance supplier list

Requirement: Makes sure information and licensed software are removed from equipment before it is disposed of or re-used.
What good looks like: Disposal procedure and approved providers; Destruction or erasure certificates matched to asset records

Requirement: Protects information stored on, processed by or accessible through laptops, desktops, phones and tablets — the devices most exposed to loss, theft and malware.
What good looks like: Endpoint policy and device baseline; Management console reports: encryption, patch level, compliance status

Requirement: Restricts and closely manages privileged access — administrator and other powerful rights — because misuse or compromise of these accounts does the most damage.
What good looks like: Privileged account inventory with owners and approvals; MFA enforcement on privileged accounts

Requirement: Restricts access to information and application functions in line with the access control policy, so people see and do only what their role requires.
What good looks like: Permission configurations for key applications and file shares; Access matrices compared with actual settings

Requirement: Protects source code, development tools and software libraries from unauthorised access and change, preventing tampering and leakage of intellectual property.
What good looks like: Repository access lists and branch protection settings; Secret scanning configuration and alerts

Requirement: Implements authentication strong enough for the risk of what is being accessed — with multi-factor authentication for remote, privileged and sensitive access.
What good looks like: Identity provider MFA policies and coverage reports; Login protection settings

Requirement: Monitors and plans the capacity of systems, networks and people so services do not fail from running out of resources.
What good looks like: Capacity monitoring dashboards and alerts; Capacity plans or forecasts

Requirement: Protects against malware with technical controls supported by user awareness — prevention, detection and response together.
What good looks like: Endpoint protection coverage and health reports; Email and web filtering configurations

Requirement: Finds technical vulnerabilities in a timely way, assesses the exposure they create and fixes them based on risk.
What good looks like: Vulnerability scan coverage and results; Remediation SLAs and tracking against them

Requirement: Establishes, documents and enforces secure configurations for hardware, software, services and networks — and detects when systems drift from them.
What good looks like: Documented baselines and hardening standards; Configuration compliance or posture reports

Requirement: Deletes information when it is no longer needed, so the organisation does not keep data — and risk — longer than necessary.
What good looks like: Deletion procedures tied to retention rules; Deletion logs or supplier deletion confirmations

Requirement: Masks, pseudonymises or anonymises sensitive data where full values are not needed — especially in testing, analytics and support.
What good looks like: Masking rules or standards; Configuration showing masked fields in applications and test data

Requirement: Detects and prevents unauthorised disclosure of sensitive information through email, web uploads, removable media, printing and other channels.
What good looks like: DLP policy and rule configurations; DLP alert records and investigations

Requirement: Keeps backup copies of information, software and systems, and proves they can be restored — so data loss is recoverable.
What good looks like: Backup policy and schedules per system; Backup job success reports

Requirement: Builds enough redundancy into systems and facilities to meet availability requirements, removing single points of failure that matter.
What good looks like: Architecture diagrams showing redundancy; Failover test results

Requirement: Produces, protects and keeps logs of activity, exceptions and events — the raw material for detecting incidents and investigating them afterwards.
What good looks like: Logging standard listing events per system type; Central log platform configuration and retention settings

Requirement: Watches networks, systems and applications for anomalous behaviour and acts on it, so potential incidents are detected while they can still be contained.
What good looks like: Monitoring scope and use cases; Alert handling records and response times

Requirement: Synchronises system clocks to an approved time source, so logs from different systems can be correlated reliably during investigations.
What good looks like: Time synchronisation configuration on key systems; Drift monitoring results

Requirement: Restricts and controls utility programs that can override system and application controls, because they can bypass security entirely.
What good looks like: List of approved privileged utilities and who may use them; Logs of utility use

Requirement: Controls software installation on operational systems so only approved, tested software runs in production.
What good looks like: Software installation rules and approved software list; Change records for production installations

Requirement: Secures and manages networks and network devices to protect the information passing through them and the systems connected to them.
What good looks like: Network diagrams and firewall rule sets; Network device configuration and patch status

Requirement: Identifies the security mechanisms, service levels and requirements for network services — internal or provided by suppliers — and makes sure they are delivered.
What good looks like: Network service agreements with security requirements; Provider performance and security reports

Requirement: Separates groups of services, users and systems into different network segments, limiting how far an attacker or fault can spread.
What good looks like: Network segmentation design; Inter-segment firewall rules

Requirement: Manages access to external websites to reduce exposure to malicious content and enforce acceptable use.
What good looks like: Web filtering policy and category settings; Coverage for remote users

Requirement: Defines and applies rules for using cryptography effectively — including key management — to protect confidentiality, integrity and authenticity.
What good looks like: Cryptography policy and approved algorithms list; Key management procedures and key inventory

Requirement: Builds security into every stage of software and system development, rather than testing it in at the end.
What good looks like: Secure development policy or SDLC description; Developer training records

Requirement: Identifies, specifies and approves security requirements when developing or acquiring applications, so security is part of what "done" means.
What good looks like: Security requirements in specifications or user stories; Procurement criteria for third-party applications

Requirement: Defines and applies principles for engineering secure systems — such as defence in depth and least privilege — across development and integration work.
What good looks like: Documented security architecture principles; Architecture review records referencing them

Requirement: Applies secure coding practices so software is written without common vulnerabilities in the first place.
What good looks like: Secure coding standards; Static analysis and dependency scan results in the pipeline

Requirement: Tests security during development and before acceptance, so vulnerabilities are found and fixed before systems go live.
What good looks like: Security test plans and results; Acceptance sign-offs including security

Requirement: Directs, monitors and reviews outsourced development so the code delivered meets your security requirements.
What good looks like: Outsourcing contracts with security clauses; Supplier security test results and code review records

Requirement: Separates development, test and production environments to reduce the risk of unauthorised or accidental changes to production systems and data.
What good looks like: Environment architecture showing separation; Access lists per environment

Requirement: Controls changes to systems and information processing facilities so they are assessed, approved, tested and reversible — and do not quietly weaken security.
What good looks like: Change management procedure; Change records with approvals, tests and rollback plans

Requirement: Selects, protects and manages the information used for testing, so test environments do not become an easy route to sensitive data.
What good looks like: Test data rules and approvals for production data use; Masking or synthetic data tooling

Requirement: Plans and agrees audit tests and other assurance activities on operational systems so they do not disrupt services or expose information.
What good looks like: Audit and test plans agreed with management; Auditor access records and removal
